column3: What is a salt, and what does it defeat?
column4: Random data mixed in before hashing, stored alongside the result. It defeats rainbow tables: one precomputed chart can no longer crack everybody at once.
A precomputed fingerprint→input lookup. It works because an unsalted hash of the same input is the same for everyone — a salt makes each search independent.

column3: monk-mode's salt: size, scope, and its own stated reason?
column4: 16 bytes, FRESH PER CODE, from a CSPRNG. Its comment: "The per-code salt makes each block's offline search independent and rainbow-tables useless."

column3: What is a KDF and why is it deliberately slow?
column4: A key derivation function: a slow, salted hash for secrets humans handle. SHA-256 does billions/sec on a GPU — for a guessable code, fast is the ATTACKER's friend.
PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 · 600,000 iterations · 16-byte salt · 32-byte output. All three pinned by unit tests so a retune is "one loud edit".
≈0.39 s on this machine. You pay it ONCE per code check; the attacker pays it PER GUESS. Against a 10-char code from a 32-symbol alphabet that is the whole defence.

column3: What does a MAC add over a plain hash?
column4: A key. Anyone can hash anything, so a bare hash proves nothing against an attacker who can recompute it. A MAC is a wax seal whose stamp only you own — anyone can see it, nobody else can forge it.
The standard construction for building a MAC out of a hash function. HMAC-SHA256 = a keyed signature built on SHA-256.
HMAC-SHA256 over the canonical string's Unicode (UTF-16LE) bytes, Base64-encoded, keyed with a 32-byte per-block random key.
The same text HMAC'd as UTF-16LE and as UTF-8 gives COMPLETELY different MACs. .NET's Encoding.Unicode means UTF-16LE, not UTF-8 — cross-language reimplementations die here.
Turning data into ONE exact string before signing it — same fields, same order, same formatting, every time. No canonical form, no meaningful signature.
`Name=value` one per line, `\n`-terminated, in a FIXED order, built from the DECRYPTED values so it's byte-identical whoever writes it.

column3: Why must every protected field be inside the canonical?
column4: A field OUTSIDE the canonical is a field an attacker may freely edit — the MAC still verifies. Coverage is the protection.

column3: The AllSessionKill example — what would omitting it allow?
column4: Flipping an armed all-session block back to session-0-only, then running a blocked app in a second logged-in session. Inside the canonical, that edit fails the MAC instead.

column3: Why is gluing fields (`"Until=" + u + "Committed=" + c`) forgeable?
column4: A value can contain the separator and swallow its neighbour, so two DIFFERENT field-sets produce the SAME string — and therefore the same valid MAC. One MAC, two meanings.
Sign a form that can only be read one way. Ambiguity in the signed representation is a hole no matter how strong the cipher is.

Learning a secret from how LONG an operation takes, without ever seeing it. `==` stops at the first differing byte, so a closer guess is rejected fractionally slower — repeat and recover the MAC byte by byte.
.NET: CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals over the raw bytes. Python: hmac.compare_digest. Always compare everything; never exit early.
Fail-closed = if the check breaks, DENY (a blocker must). Fail-open = if the check breaks, allow — how convenience wins and security dies.

column3: What does ConfigMacIsValid do on a blank/malformed/non-Base64 MAC?
column4: Returns False, never throws. Any verification failure leaves the block STANDING — the safe state is chosen on doubt, always.

column3: What is DPAPI machine scope protecting here, and what doesn't it protect against?
column4: Windows encrypts the 32-byte HMAC key so only THIS machine can decrypt it. It's a safe bolted to the building — no use against someone who has the building.

column3: Why is Simple3Des documented-weak-by-design and still a correct decision?
column4: Because the threat is TAMPERING, not secrecy. Confidentiality of a file the user already owns buys almost nothing; the HMAC layer above does the real work.
Name your threat model, then spend your strength where the threat is. Crypto misused as decoration is worse than none — it buys false confidence.
TypeError — number-meets-text always errors. + adds (both numbers) or glues (both strings); it never mixes.

column3: What does a function return if no return statement ever runs?
column4: None — every call hands back something; no return hit → None. (print instead of return is the classic cause.)
return hands a value back (usable, storable, testable); print only paints pixels. The print version returns None.

column3: Phrase for "string contains at least one digit"?
column4: any(ch.isdigit() for ch in pw) — pw.isdigit() asks "is the WHOLE string digits?", the wrong question.

column3: What does any(...) take and give back?
column4: Takes a stream of booleans, gives one: True if at least one is True. Without it you have many answers and no verdict.

column3: Which branch of an if/elif chain runs?
column4: The FIRST true one, top to bottom — the rest are skipped even if also true. Narrowest/highest test first.
4.5, a float — numbers mix freely (int gets promoted); only number-meets-TEXT errors.

column3: Fix is right but the checker still fails — first check?
column4: Is the file SAVED? The checker runs what's on disk. VS Code: ● on the tab = unsaved.
